section.title: Introduction and Overview
section.p: Impression is a desktop publishing application for RISC OS, produced by Computer Concepts. This chapter describes the on-disk format of an Impression document, as reconstructed from the source of the TransIMP converter, a loader that reads Impression documents and produces OvationPro DDL (Document Description Language) output for import into OvationPro. Impression's own file format was never published, so this description is derived entirely from what a working converter needs to read correctly; it is not a specification released by the format's authors.

Because the format is reconstructed rather than specified, many fields have no confirmed purpose: the converter parses them, or skips past them, without needing to know what they mean. Every field described in this chapter states whether its purpose is confirmed by converter behaviour, inferred from its name or position, or entirely unknown. Fields with no established purpose are marked accordingly rather than omitted, so that a reader attempting a fuller implementation knows exactly what remains to be determined.

p.fixme: Substantial areas of the format, in particular much of the file header, several bitfields in the frame and style records, and a handful of the inline text control codes, remain unidentified. A consolidated list of these gaps appears in "Unresolved and Undocumented Areas" at the end of this chapter.

section.p: An Impression document is built from several linked tables, all addressed by byte offset from a common base:

list.item: a fixed-size file header, giving the document's format version and the offsets of every other table;
a colour table, giving the document's named colours and colour tints;
a style table, giving up to 255 named character and paragraph styles;
a paragraph/heading numbering table, giving the numbering sequences used by automatic page, chapter, and list numbering;
an object dictionary, one entry per story (a run of text) or embedded picture, linking each to its underlying data;
a master-page object-record stream, describing the frames placed on the document's master pages;
a main-document object-record stream, describing the document's own pages, chapters, and frames; and
the text and picture data itself, either embedded within the same data block or, for larger documents, held in separate files (see "Document storage: single file versus directory mode").

definition-table.definition: A rectangular (or, for pictures, optionally irregular) region placed on a page: a text frame, picture frame, blank frame, group, or guide line. Every frame is described by an object record in an object-record stream.
The text content flowing through one or more linked text frames, or the picture data displayed by one or more linked picture frames. Every story has an entry in the object dictionary.

A document is divided into one or more sections, each associated with a pair of master pages and holding its own run of main pages. Impression's own user interface calls these "chapters"; the on-disk object type is XSECT.
A template page, edited separately from the document's main pages, whose frames are automatically linked to corresponding frames on every main page that uses it.
The array of dictstr records (see "Object Dictionary") that indexes every story and embedded picture in the document.

Internal converter terms, not document fields: an "epoch" numbers successive chapters so that repeated instances of the same master-page frame receive distinct output identifiers (see "Frame identifiers and epochs"); a "generation" numbers successive repetitions of a repeating frame.

subsection.title: Document storage: single file versus directory mode
subsection.p: An Impression document can be stored in either of two ways, both described by the same header and table layout:

item.p: As a single file. The whole of the structure described in this chapter, including all text and picture data, is held as one contiguous block, read entirely into memory. All offsets in the file header, and all offsets embedded within object records, are byte offsets from the start of this block.

As a directory (an Impression "application directory" style document). The directory contains a file called !DocData, holding the same header and table structure as the single-file case, but the offset-addressed tables within it (colours, styles, numbering, the object dictionary, and the master-page and main-page object-record streams) are used purely as an in-memory index: the bulk data for each story and picture is held in separate files, described in "Directory layout and story files" under "Object Dictionary".

subsection.p: A converter can distinguish the two cases by examining the input path: if it names a directory rather than a file, directory mode applies and the actual data file to open first is !DocData within it.

subsection.title: Object-record streams
subsection.p: Several of the document's major tables (the master-page frames, the main-document pages/chapters/frames, and by convention the picture and text data referenced from the object dictionary) are stored as a stream of variable-length object records, all sharing the same eight-byte header format (see "Object record header"). Each record begins with a type code and a total length (header included); the stream is walked by repeatedly reading the length, stopping when a record of length zero is encountered, and advancing to the next record by adding the current record's length to the current position:

Frame objects (XTEXT, XPICT, XBLANK, XGUIDE, XGROUP) additionally carry a "level" value (see "Frame flags word") giving their front-to-back stacking position; a run of consecutive frames sharing a level and a non-zero group number belong to the same group (XGROUP) object.

subsection.title: Frame identifiers and epochs
subsection.p: The converter identifies every frame, picture, and text story in its DDL output by a hexadecimal offset relative to the start of the in-memory document data block. Because a master page's frames are reused, unmodified, by every main page that references that master page, a plain byte offset would collide across chapters. The converter avoids this by numbering each chapter with a successive "epoch": when generating an identifier for a master-page frame in the context of a particular chapter, it adds epoch_number * contents2 (see "File Header") to the frame's raw offset, where contents2 is comfortably larger than the document data block itself, guaranteeing the result cannot collide with a genuine offset into the block. The same mechanism, using a "generation" counter instead of an epoch, distinguishes successive repetitions of a repeating frame (see "Text Story Data").

section.title: File Header
section.p: Every Impression document (or, in directory mode, its !DocData file) begins with a fixed-size header of 380 bytes. The header gives the document's format version and the byte offsets of every other table described in this chapter. Unless stated otherwise, all multi-byte fields are little-endian, matching normal ARM/RISC OS byte order, and all offset fields are byte offsets measured from the start of this header (offset 0).

The first three words identify and version the document; a converter should refuse a document whose version word is below 28, which the TransIMP converter treats as "too old a version of Impression" to convert reliably.

offset-table.offset: Unknown. Varies between documents (unlike v2, below), so is not itself a format signature; possibly a checksum or a per-document identifier.

A fixed signature word, 0x12345678, confirmed identical across an empirical survey of 46 real Impression documents of varying age and authorship. Not validated by this converter (a document with a different value here is simply unconfirmed, not necessarily invalid), but consistent enough to treat as a format-identification magic number.
Document format version number. The converter refuses to proceed if this is less than 28 (the minimum version it supports).
Unknown; reserved block.
Unknown.
Unknown; reserved block.
Offset to the start of the on-disk colour table (an array of icolourstr records; see "Colour Table").

Not referenced by the conversion source. Empirically always exactly equal to colour1 (0 exceptions across a 46-document survey), suggesting this is a duplicate copy of that field rather than an independently meaningful offset, though the reason for the duplication is unconfirmed.
Not referenced by the conversion source. Empirically always exactly equal to colour1, in the same way as colour2, above.

Offset to the end of the colour table (colour1 .. tints spans the icolourstr array). Despite the name, both base colours and colour tints are stored together in this one array; see "Colour Table". Unlike colour2/colour3, this field genuinely diverges from colour1 in practice (5 of 46 surveyed documents), confirming it as a real, distinct boundary rather than a further duplicate.
Base offset of the style table: a 255-entry array of 4-byte offsets, each relative to this field, one per style slot (see "Character and Paragraph Styles").

Not referenced by the conversion source. Empirically always exactly equal to numbers (offset 308), across a 46-document survey, in the same manner as x4 and x5 below; the reason for the apparent quadruplication of that one value across x3, x4, x5, and numbers is unconfirmed.
Not referenced by the conversion source. Empirically always exactly equal to numbers (offset 308); see x3.
Not referenced by the conversion source. Empirically always exactly equal to numbers (offset 308); see x3.
Offset to the start of the paragraph/heading numbering table (an array of numberstr records; see "Paragraph and Heading Numbering").

Offset to the end of the numbering table (numbers .. x7 spans the numberstr array). The field is named generically in the source, but its role as the numbering table's end offset is established by the converter's own size calculation.
Unknown; not referenced by the conversion source.
Unknown; not referenced by the conversion source.
Unknown; not referenced by the conversion source.

Offset to the start of the object dictionary (an array of dictstr records; see "Object Dictionary"). The array's end boundary is mdict1, below -- confirmed directly from the conversion source -- not dict2.

Not exercised by the conversion source. An empirical 46-document survey found it always exactly equal to dict1 itself (0 exceptions), so it behaves as a duplicate of dict1. It is not the dictionary array's end boundary; that role belongs to mdict1, below.

Offset to the "master dictionary": an array of file-offset integers, one per object-dictionary entry plus one trailing sentinel entry, giving the byte offset within the original input file at which each dictionary entry's story or picture data begins (see "Object Dictionary"). Also confirmed, directly from the conversion source, as the object dictionary's end boundary: the number of dictionary entries is (mdict1 - dict1) / 56.

Not exercised by the conversion source. As with dict2, an empirical 46-document survey found it always exactly equal to mdict1, so it behaves as a duplicate of mdict1 rather than an end-of-array partner.
Offset to the start of the master-page object-record stream (see "Object-record streams").

Not referenced by the conversion source. The master-page stream is actually walked from masterpages1 up to (but excluding) mainpages1, so masterpages2 is not the stream's end-of-range partner. An empirical 46-document survey instead found it always exactly equal to masterpages1, so it behaves as a duplicate of masterpages1.

End boundary (exclusive) of the master-page object-record stream: the stream is walked from masterpages1 up to this offset. Empirically always exactly equal to mainpages2 (below) across a 46-document survey; see the note following this table.
Offset to the start of the main document's page/frame object-record stream (see "Object-record streams"). Empirically always exactly equal to mainpages1, above.

End boundary (exclusive) of the main document's page/frame object-record stream: the stream is walked from mainpages2 up to this offset, and a converter should treat any object record reaching or passing this offset as a corrupt document. Empirically always exactly equal to contents2 (below) across a 46-document survey, consistent with nothing else occupying the document-data block after the end of this stream.

Total length, in bytes, of the document data block described by this header (the whole of !DocData, or the equivalent initial chunk read from a single-file document). Used both to size the in-memory copy of the document and, multiplied by a chapter's epoch number, as the stride used to build unique frame identifiers for repeated master-page instances (see "Frame identifiers and epochs").
Character string. Consistent with a previous filename recorded for the document, for example one retained across a Save As operation, though this is not read anywhere in the conversion source.

section.p: An empirical survey of 46 real Impression documents (of varying age and authorship, produced outside this project) found mainpages1 and mainpages2 exactly equal in every case, meaning the master-page object-record stream is immediately followed by the main-document object-record stream with no gap between them in practice. The same survey found several other offset-table pairs always exactly equal to each other with no exceptions: colour1/colour2/colour3, x3/x4/x5/numbers, dict1/dict2, mdict1/mdict2, masterpages1/masterpages2, and contents1/contents2 (see the individual field descriptions above). Only colour1 and tints were found to genuinely diverge, confirming that pair as a real, distinct start/end boundary rather than a duplicated field. This does not prove the fields that were always found equal can never diverge in some other document, but no example examined so far contradicts treating colour2, colour3, x3, x4, x5, dict2, mdict2, and masterpages2 as duplicates of their respective sibling field, rather than as independently meaningful offsets.

subsection.title: Object record header
subsection.p: Every record in an object-record stream (see "Object-record streams") begins with this eight-byte header, followed immediately by a type-specific body.

offset-table.offset: Object type code; see the following table.
Unknown.

Unknown.
Unknown.
Low 8 bits of the record's total length (header included); see len1.
High 8 bits of the record's total length. The full 16-bit length is len0 + (len1 << 8); a length of zero terminates the enclosing object-record stream.
Unknown.

value-table.value: Page. See "Page object (XPAGE)".
Text frame. See "Text, blank, guide, and group frames".
Picture frame. See "Picture frame (XPICT)".
Blank frame (an unlinked frame that may later become text or picture). See "Text, blank, guide, and group frames".
Not defined by the conversion source; unused/unknown.
Branch. See "Branch object (XBRANCH)".
Section (chapter). See "Section object (XSECT)".
Not defined by the conversion source; unused/unknown.
Page guide line. See "Text, blank, guide, and group frames".
Frame group. See "Text, blank, guide, and group frames".
Not defined by the conversion source; unused/unknown.

Recognised locally by the converter as an unidentified frame type, tolerated (and otherwise ignored) rather than treated as an error; the source notes this type has been observed in corrupt documents. An empirical 46-document survey found six real instances (across four separate documents), every one with an identical 28-byte body -- a consistent size across independent documents is not what random corruption would produce, so this more likely represents a genuine, structured object kind that this converter's era simply never learned to interpret, rather than damage. Its body format remains undecoded.

Byte value 0xFF, read as the signed value -1. Treated as equivalent to XBLANK everywhere it is tested, suggesting it is an alternate or legacy blank-frame type code rather than a distinct object kind.

subsection.title: Frame object common layout
subsection.p: The XTEXT, XBLANK, XGUIDE, and XGROUP object bodies share an identical 104-byte layout, described here once. The XPICT body begins with the same 104 bytes and then extends it (see "Picture frame (XPICT)").

offset-table.offset: Unknown.
Left edge of the frame's outer box, in the document's drawing-coordinate units.
Bottom edge of the frame's outer box.
Right edge of the frame's outer box.
Top edge of the frame's outer box.
Packed flags word; see "Frame flags word".

Index into the object dictionary (see "Object Dictionary") identifying this frame's associated story or picture data; negative when the frame has no associated story, for example an unlinked blank frame.
Left edge of the frame's "repel" outer box, used for text-flow avoidance around the frame by frames elsewhere on the page.
Bottom edge of the repel box.
Right edge of the repel box.
Top edge of the repel box.
Unknown.

A tag value shared with the corresponding frame on the linked master page, not a positional index despite the name: the conversion source (ixindex() in c/frames.c) resolves a main-document frame's master counterpart by scanning the frames on the chapter's current master page for the one whose own masterindex field equals this one's, i.e. equality of a shared identifier, not lookup by stream position. Meaningful only when the "master" flag bit is set (see "Frame flags word"); the search is scoped to a single master page's own frames (bounded by the next XPAGE/XBRANCH/XSECT record) and does not resolve further if that page's frame is itself flagged as linked to a master (there is no third level).
Unknown.
Unknown.
Inline colour value word for the frame's fill colour; see "Inline colour value words". Meaningful only when the "filled" flag bit is set.
Horizontal inset margin between the frame's outer box and its text/content area.
Vertical inset margin.
Border style for one edge of the frame; 0xFF means no border is drawn on that edge, any other value indicates a border is present. See the note below.
Border style for another edge; see border0.
Border style for another edge; see border0.
Border style for the remaining edge; see border0.
Inline colour value word for the border; see "Inline colour value words". A value of -1 means no colour override (a default colour is used).

Non-zero tag value. Frames with a non-zero embedtag are anchored inline within a text story, at the point a matching CTRL_S embedded-object marker occurs (see "Text Story Data"), rather than being placed directly on the page in normal front-to-back order.
Group number this frame belongs to, meaningful when the "grouped" flag bit is set (see "Frame flags word"); 0 = not grouped.
Continuation of the flags word begun at byte 72; see "Frame group flags word".
Unknown; reserved block of seven 32-bit words.

subsection.p: The exact meaning of a non-0xFF border value, and the mapping of border0..border3 to the frame's physical top, left, bottom, and right edges, could not be established with confidence from the conversion source. The converter reorders them as (border0, border2, border3, border1) when building a four-bit edge-presence mask for its own output, which rules out a simple clockwise or "top, left, bottom, right" ordering, but does not by itself reveal the true one.

subsubsection.title: Frame flags word
subsubsection.p: The 32-bit word at offset 20 (see "Frame object common layout") packs the following bits, numbered from bit 0 as the least significant bit of the first byte read from the file:

bitfield-table.bit: Frame is currently selected in the Impression editor. Editor UI state; not relevant to conversion.
Text in other frames should flow around (repel from) this frame.
Frame has a fill colour; backcolour is meaningful.
Unknown.
This frame is linked to a corresponding frame on its master page; masterindex is meaningful.
Frame is locked against editing.
Unknown.
For XPICT frames only, this bit is "usepsscreen": use a custom PostScript halftone screen (see "Picture frame (XPICT)"). For all other frame types, this bit position is unknown.
Unknown.
Frame belongs to a frame group; groupn (offset 72) is meaningful.
Frame repeats itself; see "Text Story Data" for how repeating frames are handled.
Unknown.
Front-to-back stacking level of the frame (0 upwards). Used to determine group membership and drawing order when walking the object-record stream.

subsubsection.title: Frame group flags word
subsubsection.p: The 32-bit word beginning at offset 72 (the byte after groupn) packs the following bits:

bitfield-table.bit: Group number; see "Frame object common layout".
Unknown.
Frame's fill colour is printed in overprint mode.
Unknown, except for XPICT frames; see "Picture frame (XPICT)" for the two bits this word carries in that case.

offset-table.offset: Unknown.
Left edge of the page's outer box.
Bottom edge of the page's outer box.
Right edge of the page's outer box.
Top edge of the page's outer box.
Unknown.
Unknown.
Page bleed margin. Subtracted from the outer box on all sides to give the media/print box: width = (x1-x0) - 2*bleed, height = (y1-y0) - 2*bleed.
Unknown.
Unknown.

Name of the master page, as a character string. Not read anywhere in the conversion source, which derives master-page linkage purely from a section's mpindex field and positional matching instead (see "Section object (XSECT)").

subsection.title: Text, blank, guide, and group frames
subsection.p: The bodies of XTEXT, XBLANK, XGUIDE, and XGROUP object records all use exactly the common 104-byte layout given in "Frame object common layout", with no type-specific extension. The four types differ only in how the converter interprets the shared fields:

list.item: XTEXT is a normal text frame; its story (via dictionaryindex) holds formatted text, described in "Text Story Data".

XBLANK is an unlinked frame, not yet assigned as text or picture; on a main page it may still carry a dictionaryindex if it has been linked to a story, and its master-page counterpart (if any) determines whether it behaves as a text or picture frame once instantiated.

XGUIDE is a non-printing page guide line. Only x0, y0, x1, y1, locked, and level (from the common layout) are meaningful; a single XGUIDE record produces four independent guide lines in the output (the frame's left, right, bottom, and top edges). No XGUIDE record was found in an empirical 46-document survey, so this type is unconfirmed against real data; it is possible guide lines are simply not persisted to disk by any Impression version represented in that survey.

XGROUP marks the end of a run of grouped frames sharing the same level and group number; it carries the group's own master-page linkage (via the master bit and masterindex) but does not itself describe a drawable frame.

subsection.title: Picture frame (XPICT)
subsection.p: The XPICT object body begins with the same 104-byte common layout given in "Frame object common layout" (with bit 16 of the frame flags word repurposed as usepsscreen, and offset 72's flags word carrying two extra bits, both described below), and extends it to a fixed 160 bytes as follows:

offset-table.offset: Horizontal scale factor for the picture. Stored as the reciprocal of the displayed horizontal scale; 0x10000 represents unity scale.
Vertical scale factor, using the same reciprocal convention as xscale.
Horizontal origin shift for the picture within its frame.
Vertical origin shift for the picture within its frame.
Rotation angle, in degrees multiplied by 0x10000 (16.16 fixed-point degrees).

Packed word: lpi (halftone screen ruling, in lines per inch), psscreen (halftone screen angle or identifier), and psx0 (remaining bits, unknown). All three are meaningful only when the usepsscreen flag bit is set. The exact byte order of this word could not be confirmed: the source's own inline comments for lpi and psscreen give offsets in the opposite order to their declaration, suggesting the original author was themselves unsure of the precise layout. No picture frame with usepsscreen set was found in an empirical 46-document survey, so this remains untested against real data either way.
Unknown; reserved block of eight 32-bit words.

subsection.p: The two extra bits carried in the frame group flags word (offset 72; see "Frame group flags word") for XPICT records only are:

bitfield-table.bit: Unknown.
Use the picture's recommended/preferred screening settings rather than the explicit lpi/psscreen values.
Unknown.

subsubsection.title: Irregular boundary (crop path) data
subsubsection.p: When an XPICT object record's total length (from the object record header) exceeds the fixed 160-byte body, the additional bytes hold a sequence of tagged extension sub-records. Each sub-record begins with a 32-bit code word: if the low byte of the code is 1, the sub-record is an irregular boundary (crop/clip path) and is decoded as described below; for any other low-byte value, the scanner skips forward to the next sub-record by (code >> 8) bytes minus 4 (the code's upper 24 bits, less the 4 bytes of the code word already read). No other sub-record kind is interpreted by the converter, so their low-byte tag values and payload formats are undetermined. No XPICT record with a body extending beyond the fixed 160 bytes was found in an empirical 46-document survey, so this whole mechanism -- irregular boundaries and any other extension sub-record kind alike -- is unconfirmed against real data; it is implemented exactly as read from the conversion source, but by construction only synthetic test fixtures currently exercise it.
The irregular boundary sub-record's payload, following its code word, is a path made of a sequence of 32-bit opcodes:

value-table.value: End of path.
Move to (x, y): followed by two 32-bit signed coordinates. Coordinates are stored relative to the centre of the picture frame's outer box.
Close the current sub-path.
Curve segment. Recognised but not decoded by the converter; the shape and presence of any following payload is undetermined.
Draw (line) to (x, y): followed by two 32-bit signed coordinates, using the same centre-relative convention as opcode 2.

subsection.title: Section object (XSECT)
subsection.p: An XSECT record marks the start of a chapter: the master-page pair it uses, its page-numbering behaviour, and, following it in the stream, the run of main-page object records belonging to it (up to the next XSECT, XBRANCH, or end of stream).

offset-table.offset: Unknown.

Stable chapter creation number. Unlike the chapter's position in the document, this value does not change when chapters are reordered; in directory-mode documents it names the chapter's data directory (ChapterN; see "Directory layout and story files").
Zero-based index selecting which pair of master pages (see "Section object (XSECT)" below) this chapter uses.
Explicit starting page number for this chapter, meaningful only when the startpage bit (below) is set.

Packed bits following startpagen: startpage (override automatic page numbering with startpagen), startonright (the chapter must begin on a right-hand/recto page), copyprev (unconfirmed; not read by the converter, but plausibly copies settings from the preceding chapter, based on its name), and 13 further unknown bits.
Unknown; reserved block of sixteen 32-bit words.
Explicit starting chapter number, meaningful only when the startchap bit (below) is set.
Packed bits following startchapn: startchap (override automatic chapter numbering with startchapn), and 15 further unknown bits.
Unknown; reserved block of eight 32-bit words.

subsection.p: The pair of master pages a chapter uses (mpindex) is located by counting XPAGE records in the master-page object-record stream (see "Page object (XPAGE)"): the mpindex'th XPAGE record is the chapter's primary master page, and, if the following XPAGE record has the same top edge (y1) as the first, it is treated as a second, paired master page (giving separate left- and right-hand master pages for a double-sided chapter).

When a chapter has two paired master pages, which one applies to a given main-document page alternates strictly through the chapter's own page sequence, in document order: the first page uses the second master page if startonright is set (and a second master page exists), or the first master page otherwise; each following page then swaps to the other master page, or stays on the first if there is no second one. This alternation, and the masterindex-based matching described under "Frame object common layout", together determine which master-page frame a given main-document frame links to.

subsection.title: Branch object (XBRANCH)
subsection.p: The XBRANCH object body is a fixed 40 bytes (ten 32-bit words), all currently unidentified. The converter reads and discards these records without interpreting their content. The object type's name, together with its position alongside XSECT in the main object-record stream, suggests it marks some form of link to, or insertion point for, another document, but this could not be confirmed from the conversion source.

section.title: Colour Table
section.p: A document's colour table is a flat array of 48-byte icolourstr records, spanning the byte range colour1 to tints in the file header (see "File Header"). The array holds both named base colours and named colour tints (shades of another named colour) together; an entry's flags field distinguishes the two.

offset-table.offset: A RISC OS palette-style colour word (blue/green/red byte order, as used by OS_ReadPalette and ColourTrans), used by the converter only as a fallback/preview value. The authoritative colour value is given by the y/c/m/k fields below. For a tint entry (see "Colour flags word"), this field is present on disk but its value is never actually used by the converter: the code path that would apply it is unconditionally overwritten, later in the same routine, by copying the base colour's own resolved palette word wholesale; see "Colour channel encoding".
Packed flags; see "Colour flags word" below.
Colour-model-dependent channel byte; see "Colour channel encoding" below.
Colour-model-dependent channel byte; see "Colour channel encoding" below.
Colour-model-dependent channel byte; see "Colour channel encoding" below.
Colour-model-dependent channel byte; see "Colour channel encoding" below.
Colour name, as a character string.
Unknown.
Unknown.
Unknown.

bitfield-table.bit: When bit 1 (tint) is clear: 1 = this is a process colour, 0 = this is a spot colour.

This entry defines a tint of another named colour, rather than a base colour. When set, bits 0 and 7 of this word are not honoured: the converter reads them, but then unconditionally overwrites the whole resolved colour record with a copy of the base colour's own flags (and palette word), so a tint entry always displays with its base colour's spot/process and overprint settings, never its own. This may not be the intended behaviour, but it is what the converter actually produces.
Unknown.
Print this colour in overprint mode. See bit 1 for the tint-entry exception.

subsubsection.title: Colour channel encoding
subsubsection.p: For a base colour entry (the tint bit clear), the low two bits of the y byte select the colour model used by the c, m, y, and k bytes, each of which is otherwise a value in the range 0-255 scaled to a channel value:

value-table.value: RGB: red = c, green = m, blue = k.
CMYK: cyan = c, magenta = m, yellow = (y & 0xFC) (the yellow channel is packed into the upper six bits of the same byte that carries the model selector), black = k.

HSV: hue = ((k << 4) | (m >> 4)), saturation = c, value = ((y >> 4) | ((m & 0xF) << 4)), each then scaled the same way as the other models (hue additionally has no /255 scaling applied, unlike saturation and value). Hue and value are each packed across the nibbles of two adjacent bytes; this is reproduced exactly from the conversion source but not independently confirmed against any other Impression documentation.

subsubsection.p: For a tint entry (the tint bit set), the fields carry different information: k holds the tint amount, in the range 0-128 where 128 is full strength (unmodified) and 0 is white; and a 12-bit index formed from (y >> 2) in its low six bits and (c & 0x3F) << 6 in its high six bits selects, by position, the icolourstr entry earlier in the same array that this tint is based on. This is the same index-computation formula used for the named-colour case of an inline colour value word (see "Inline colour value words"), confirming both refer to entries of this same table by zero-based index.

Only the tint's own name and its computed channel values (the base colour's channel values scaled toward white, by the tint fraction k/128, for RGB and HSV's value channel; scaled toward zero for CMYK and HSV's hue/saturation channels) are actually used from a tint entry itself. Every other displayed property -- model, spot/process, overprint, and palette word -- is inherited unchanged from the base colour, per the note on bit 1 in "Colour flags word".

subsection.title: Inline colour value words
subsection.p: Wherever a colour is referenced from a frame or style record (for example a frame's backcolour or bordercolour, or a style's foreground/background/underline colour), it is given as a single 32-bit "colour value word", a distinct and more compact encoding from the colour table's own icolourstr records. Reading the word as four bytes b0 (most significant) to b3 (least significant), the low two bits of b3 select how the rest of the word is interpreted:

value-table.value: RGB, given directly: red = b2, green = b1, blue = b0, each scaled from 0-255 to the colour system's internal 0-0x10000 range (multiplied by 0x10000 and divided by 255).

CMYK, given directly: cyan = b2, magenta = b1, yellow = (b3 & 0xFC), black = b0. Cyan, magenta, and black are scaled by 0x10000/255 as usual, but yellow is instead scaled by 0x10000/0xFC (0xFC being the largest value the masked byte can hold) -- unlike icolourstr's on-disk colour-table entries, which scale their equivalent yellow channel by 0x10000/255 like every other channel. This asymmetry is reproduced exactly from the conversion source. As in icolourstr, the yellow channel is packed into the upper six bits of the byte that also carries the model selector.
HSV, given directly, with hue, saturation, and value packed across nibbles of b0-b2 in the same manner as icolourstr's HSV encoding.

A reference to a named colour already defined in the document's colour table, rather than an inline value. The referenced entry's zero-based index into the icolourstr array (colour1 in the file header) is (b2 << 6) | (b3 >> 2).

section.title: Character and Paragraph Styles
section.p: A document's style table holds up to 255 named character and paragraph styles, addressed via the stylebase field in the file header (see "File Header"). stylebase points to an array of 255 four-byte offsets, one per style slot numbered 0 to 254, each relative to stylebase itself; a zero offset means the corresponding slot is unused. Style slot 0 is reserved for the document's base "body text" style: it is always treated as though every optional field described below were present, regardless of its own stored presence flags, and the converter emits it under the fixed name "BodyText" regardless of what name (if any) is actually stored in it. Slots 1-254 are the document's ordinary named styles, as created through Impression's own style-editing interface, and are selected within text stories by the low byte of a CTRL_G or CTRL_H control code (see "Text Story Data").

subsection.title: Style record fixed header (stylestr)
subsection.p: Each non-empty style slot points to a fixed 56-byte header, followed immediately by a variable-length block of optional field data whose layout is controlled by the header's own presence-flag bits (see "Style record variable data").

offset-table.offset: Presence-flags word 1; see "Style presence-flags word 1".
Presence-flags word 2; see "Style presence-flags word 2".
Bitmask, one bit per tab-stop slot (32 slots, numbered 0-31 from the least significant bit). A set bit means that tab-stop's position word is present in the variable data.
Unknown. The source comments this field with "see non-zero for efx", suggesting a link to the iseffect flag or to character "effect" styles generally.
Unknown; see xxx4.
RISC OS key code assigned as this style's keyboard shortcut (9 bits used); see "Keyboard Shortcut Encoding".

Continuation of the flags word begun at byte 20: b1 (7 bits, unknown), b2 (8 bits, unknown), and five further single-bit unknown flags, followed by paragraphapply (style applies to a whole paragraph rather than a run of selected characters), contents (unconfirmed; plausibly marks a style used to build a table-of-contents entry), and index (unconfirmed; plausibly marks a style used to build an index entry).
Style name, as a character string.

subsubsection.title: Style presence-flags word 1
subsubsection.p: Each bit, when set, means the corresponding one-byte field is present in the variable data described in "Style record variable data" (fields are listed here in bit, and therefore storage, order):

bitfield-table.bit: Unknown (xxx100).
Style automatically indents following text, for example after a bullet or number. Decoded by the converter but not reproduced in its output.
Unknown (xxx102-xxx106).
Unconfirmed selector related to the style's font; the font's actual name is carried separately (see fontname1 in "Style presence-flags word 2"). Decoded but not reproduced in the output.
Text is underlined.
Text is subscript or superscript.
Text has strikeout.
Paragraph alignment is set (0 = left, ... 3 = justified, per the source's own comment).
Unconfirmed pagination "keep" option. Decoded but not reproduced.
Unconfirmed pagination "keep" option. Decoded but not reproduced.
Automatic hyphenation setting is present.
Unknown (xxx115).
Decimal tab character is present.
Unconfirmed; plausibly "keep with next paragraph". Decoded but not reproduced.

Unconfirmed flag paired with the textcolour1 field's colour value (see "Style record variable data"). Decoded but not reproduced directly; the paired colour word governs the actual foreground colour output.
Unknown (xxx119).
Underline/strikeout colour is present. Governs both underline and strikeout colour output; see "Style record variable data" for its two-part layout.
Unknown (xxx121, xxx122).
Character/paragraph background colour is present, paired with the textcolour2 field's colour value.
Text is locked to the page's baseline grid.
Unconfirmed rule-related flag. Decoded but not reproduced.
Text is italic.
Text is bold.
This style is a character "effect" style rather than a full named style; affects whether background/foreground colours are honoured (see "Style record variable data").
Unconfirmed; the source comments this "ruler related".
Style is shown on Impression's style-selection menu.
Unknown (xxx131).
Left indent value is present.
Right indent value is present.
First-line indent value is present.
Subscript/superscript vertical offset is present. Decoded but not reproduced.
Subscript/superscript size scale is present. Decoded but not reproduced.
Line spacing (leading) value is present.
Space-after-paragraph value is present.
Space-before-paragraph value is present.
Underline vertical offset (variant 0) is present. Decoded but not reproduced.
Underline vertical offset (variant 1) is present. Decoded but not reproduced.
Unconfirmed. Decoded but not reproduced.
Unknown (xxx211, xxx212).
Font size value is present.
Font horizontal/vertical aspect scale is present.
Unknown (xxx215).
Unconfirmed; the field's name suggests "keep paragraph lines together". Decoded but not reproduced.
Tab-leader fill character is present.
Unknown (xxx218-xxx220).
Font (family and style) name is present, both as a placeholder word in sequence and as a following 40-byte string; see "Style record variable data".
Character tracking (letter-spacing) value is present.
Unknown (xxx223).
Foreground text colour is present; see "Style record variable data" for its two-part layout.
Background text colour is present, honoured only when textbackcolour (word 1) is also set and the style is not an effect style.
Unknown (xxx226-xxx231).

subsection.title: Style record variable data
subsection.p: Immediately following the 56-byte stylestr header, a style record continues with a variable-length block of optional fields. Each field's presence is controlled by the correspondingly-named bit in one of the two presence-flags words (see above), and, when present, fields appear in exactly the declaration order used throughout this chapter: first every present one-byte field, then (after padding to a four-byte boundary) every present four-byte field, then the tab ruler (if any tab bit is set), then the font-style name string (if fontname1 is set), and finally three trailing colour words for whichever of textcolour1, textcolour2, and underlinecolour were flagged earlier.
For style slot 0 (the body text style), every field is always treated as present, regardless of its own presence-flags bits.

subsubsection.title: One-byte fields, in order

definition-table.definition: Underline style selector; combines with the trailing underlinecolour word to produce the output underline description.
Strikeout style selector; combines with the trailing underlinecolour word.
Placeholder byte; the actual foreground colour is carried by the trailing textcolour1 word.
Placeholder byte in this position; the actual colour value is carried by a separate trailing word (see below). The same governing bit gates both pieces of data.
Placeholder byte; the actual background colour is carried by the trailing textcolour2 word.

Only consumed when reading the body style; for ordinary styles this byte is not read even if the iseffect flag bit happens to be set. This inconsistency between the declared flag bit and the field's actual consumption is noted directly in the conversion source as a known peculiarity of the format, not a mistake in the converter.
See iseffect; consumed only for the body style.
See iseffect; consumed only for the body style.
See iseffect; consumed only for the body style.

subsubsection.p: After the last one-byte field, the data is padded to the next 4-byte boundary before the four-byte fields begin.

definition-table.definition: Right indent; a positive stored value is a delta from the frame's right edge, a negative value an absolute offset (the sign determines which indent type is emitted).
First-line indent, stored as an absolute position; the emitted value is this field minus ruler0 (the left indent), giving an indent relative to the body text.
Line spacing (leading). The top bit of the stored word selects fixed leading (remaining 24 bits, minus 0x10000, is the fixed value) versus proportional/single leading (remaining 24 bits directly).
Space before the paragraph (low 24 bits used).
Decoded but not emitted in the output.
Decoded but not emitted in the output.
Font size, stored in sixteenths of a point.
Four bytes holding a short tab-leader fill-character string (up to four characters), using the same NUL-or-CR termination convention as the font-style name field below, not NUL alone.
Placeholder word in this position; the 40-byte font-style name string itself follows later (see below). The same governing bit gates both pieces of data.
Placeholder word in this position; the actual colour value is carried by a separate trailing word (see below).
Placeholder word in this position; the actual colour value is carried by a separate trailing word (see below).

subsubsection.title: Tab ruler, font name, and trailing colour words
subsubsection.p: If any of the 32 bits of the tabs field (in the fixed header) is set, or the style is the body style, a tab ruler follows: for each set bit, in bit order from 0 to 31, one four-byte word whose low byte selects the tab kind (0 = left, 1 = centre, 2 = right, 3 = decimal, any other value = a rule-line marker rather than a stop) and whose remaining 24 bits give the tab position.

If fontname1 is set (see above), a 40-byte string follows next, holding the font (family and style) name, for example "Trinity.Medium.Italic". Like the leader field above, this uses the same NUL-or-CR termination convention as other fixed-length character-string fields in this format (see, for example, oldname in "File Header"), not NUL alone: real documents were found, empirically, to leave stale trailing bytes from a previously-stored longer name past a CR terminator when a shorter name is later written into the same field, so a reader that stops only at NUL rather than at the first of either byte will corrupt the decoded name with that leftover data.
Finally, for whichever of the following governing bits were set earlier, one trailing four-byte colour word follows, in this order:

list.item: textcolour1's actual colour value, present if flags2 bit 24 (textcolour1) is set. Used as the foreground colour.

textcolour2's actual colour value, present if flags2 bit 25 (textcolour2) is set. Used as the background colour, but only honoured when textbackcolour (flags1 bit 23) is also set and the style is not an effect style.
underlinecolour's actual colour value, present if flags1 bit 20 (underlinecolour) is set. Used as the colour for both the underline and the strikeout, if either is present.

p.fixme: The conversion source notes that a further four bytes can apparently still be read after this point in some records; no field in this trailing position is identified or decoded.

section.title: Paragraph and Heading Numbering
section.p: The numbering table (numbers to x7 in the file header; see "File Header") is a flat array of 12-byte numberstr records, describing the automatic numbering sequences used by page numbers, chapter numbers, and numbered list/heading styles. Numbering sequences are scoped to an individual story (dcindex): the current value at any point in a story is found by scanning backwards through the array from the matching record to the most recent record for the same story that has its start bit set, and summing the increments seen along the way.

offset-table.offset: This record resets the running numbering sequence.
The value the sequence is reset to, when start is set (added to the running count at this point).
Numbering style; see the following table.
A per-numbering-sequence tag, matched against the tag value embedded in a CTRL_K "insert number" marker within a text story (see "Text Story Data").
Dictionary index of the text story this numbering record belongs to.

value-table.value: Decimal (1, 2, 3, ...). The only style the converter renders as formatted text.
Upper-case Roman numerals. Recognised on disk; the converter does not produce formatted output for this style, a known gap in the converter rather than an unknown format detail.
Lower-case Roman numerals. See type 1.
Upper-case letters. See type 1.
Lower-case letters. See type 1.
Bullet. See type 1.

section.title: Object Dictionary
section.p: The object dictionary (dict1 in the file header; see "File Header") is a flat array of 56-byte dictstr records, one per story or embedded picture in the document. A frame's dictionaryindex field (see "Frame object common layout") is a zero-based index into this array. The array's end boundary is confirmed directly from the conversion source (c/styles.c's checkstyles(), which walks dictstr records while their address is less than docdata+mdict1) to be mdict1, not dict2: the number of dictionary entries is (mdict1 - dict1) / 56. dict1 and mdict1 are themselves confirmed, adjacent regions of the document data block; dict2 (see "File Header") is a separate field that always duplicates dict1 and plays no part in this calculation.

offset-table.offset: Dictionary entry kind; see the following table.
Unknown.
Unknown.
Unknown.

On-disk story/data identifier. In directory-mode documents, this matches the numeric suffix of the entry's StoryN file (for a DCPICT entry) or the chunk id inside the owning chapter's Text file (for a DCTEXT entry); see "Directory layout and story files".
Unknown.
Unknown.
Unknown.
Unknown.

Unconfirmed; presumably a stored copy of the entry's data length. The converter always derives the actual length independently, from the master dictionary's offset table (mdict1 in the file header), rather than reading this field.
Unknown.
Packed foreign-file-type identification word, used for DCPICT entries holding embedded objects; see "Embedded object types" below.
Unknown.
Unknown.
Unknown.
Unknown.
Unknown.

value-table.value: A picture or other embedded (non-text) object.
A text story.
A chapter (section) marker within the dictionary, used to count chapters when locating directory-mode story files; see "Directory layout and story files".
A branch. Not otherwise interpreted by the converter.

subsection.title: Master dictionary (mdict1)
subsection.p: The master dictionary (mdict1 in the file header) is an array of 32-bit file-offset integers, one per dictionary entry plus one trailing sentinel entry. Entry N gives the byte offset, within the original input file, at which dictionary entry N's story or picture data begins; the corresponding data's length is found by subtracting entry N's offset from entry N+1's offset (which is why the array carries one more entry than there are dictionary records). This table is only used to locate data in single-file documents; in directory mode, story data is instead found by name within the document's directory structure (see "Directory layout and story files"), though the master dictionary is still consulted to compute a story's length.

subsection.title: Embedded object types
subsection.p: For a DCPICT entry, the types field's low 12 bits (or, within the 0xAFF family described below, an inner 12-bit sub-code) identify the kind of foreign data embedded at that dictionary entry:

value-table.value: EPS (Encapsulated PostScript). Given a dedicated header format; see "EPS embedded object data".

A member of the "Draw-like" application family, identified more precisely by an inner 12-bit sub-code taken from bits 12-23 of types (falling back to the outer code itself if that sub-code is zero): 0xFF9 or 0xC85 or 0xAFF itself all resolve to Draw; 0xBCF to Tablemate; 0xD91 to Equasor; 0xB98 to Formulix; 0xC37 to Eureka; 0xB84 to DiagramIt; 0xB7D to TabCalc; 0xB83 to GraphMate; any other sub-code is treated generically as "Data". These twelve-bit codes closely resemble RISC OS filetype numbers; for example, 0xAFF is the standard Draw filetype, which is consistent with a Draw file having been embedded using its native RISC OS filetype as the class code.
ArtWorks.
Treated generically as "Data": the raw bytes are embedded without a recognised application association.

subsection.p: Every one of the 104 embedded pictures found across a 46-document survey classified as Draw, and every one began with the standard RISC OS DrawFile signature and a plausible bounding box when checked. No EPS, ArtWorks, other Draw-family application, or generic "Data" picture was found in that survey, so those paths remain unconfirmed against real documents.

subsection.title: EPS embedded object data
subsection.p: An EPS-tagged story's raw data (as read from the input file or a directory-mode StoryN file) begins with a header the converter partly reads and partly leaves unexamined:

offset-table.offset: Unknown; not read by the converter.
Length, in bytes, of the actual EPS content that follows the header.
Unknown; not read by the converter.

Unknown; not read by the converter before it is overwritten. The converter reuses this part of its own read buffer, in place, to build a replacement header for its DDL output, so nothing about its original on-disk content can be recovered from the conversion source.
A null-terminated string (padded to a four-byte boundary), consistent with the embedded object's original filename or an EPS preview name.
The raw EPS content itself, length bytes long, as given by the length field at offset 12.

subsection.p: When producing its own DDL output for an EPS object, the converter constructs a fresh header of its own, distinct from the one just described: a 4-byte overall length (the replacement header's own size, rounded up to a multiple of four, plus the EPS content length), a 4-byte copy of the source's content length, and two zeroed 4-byte fields, followed by the same name string read from the source and then the EPS content itself. This output header is a converter construction for the DDL format, not a description of a second on-disk Impression structure.

subsection.title: Directory layout and story files
subsection.p: In directory-mode documents (see "Document storage: single file versus directory mode"), the bulk data referenced by the object dictionary is held in files alongside !DocData, laid out as follows:

item.p: MasterChap holds the master pages' own text and pictures: a file called Text, holding every DCTEXT chunk belonging to the master pages (see below), and one file called StoryN per DCPICT dictionary entry belonging to the master pages, where N is that entry's id field.
Each chapter has its own directory, named ChapterN where N is that chapter's createn field (see "Section object (XSECT)"), holding its own Text and StoryN files in the same way.

subsection.p: Whether a given dictionary entry belongs to the master pages or to a particular chapter is determined by counting DCSECT-typed entries in the object dictionary that precede it. The dictionary always carries one DCSECT entry for the master pages themselves, before any entry belonging to a real chapter, so exactly one preceding DCSECT entry means the entry belongs to the master pages (MasterChap) -- not zero, which does not occur in practice. Two or more preceding DCSECT entries give a zero-based chapter index (two -> chapter 0, three -> chapter 1, and so on), which is then matched against successive XSECT object records in the main object-record stream, in order, to find that chapter's createn value. This is confirmed directly from the conversion source (getifp() and chapcn() in c/frames.c) and was cross-checked empirically: across a 46-document survey, the number of DCSECT dictionary entries was always exactly one more than the number of real chapters, with no exceptions.
A chapter's Text file is a concatenation of chunks, each prefixed by an eight-byte header:

offset-table.offset: Total length of this chunk, in bytes, including this eight-byte header.
Chunk identifier, matched against a DCTEXT dictionary entry's id field.

subsection.p: A story's text is located within the file by scanning chunks sequentially from the start, comparing each chunk's id against the target dictionary entry's id, and skipping forward by (chunk length - 8) bytes whenever it does not match.

section.title: Text Story Data
section.p: A text story's data, however it is located (see "Object Dictionary"), is a sequence of line records, each beginning with an eight-byte ilinestr header:

offset-table.offset: Unknown.
Length of the preceding line record (24-bit little-endian). Not used by the converter.
Low three bits select this line record's kind; see the following table. The remaining bits are unknown; the source itself notes uncertainty here ("low nibble 1, 2 page style info? 5, normal line").
Length of this line record, including this eight-byte header (24-bit little-endian). A value of zero terminates the story.

value-table.value: Frame-reference line; see "Frame-reference lines" below.
Text-content line; see "Text-content lines" below.
Present in real documents but skipped over unread by the converter; purpose undetermined.

subsection.title: Frame-reference lines
subsection.p: A frame-reference line's payload begins with a single 32-bit integer identifying the text or blank frame through which this story's text flows at this point. It is not a docdata-absolute byte offset by itself: in a single-file document, the conversion source resolves it as masterpages1 + offset for a master-page story, or mainpages2 + offset for a main-document story (matching the file header fields of the same name; see "File Header"), not as an offset from the start of the document data block. In a directory-mode document, a main-document story's on-disk value is instead stored relative to the byte offset of the chapter's own Section (XSECT) record, and resolving it needs that record's own docdata-absolute offset added directly, with no mainpages2 term involved (a master-page story's on-disk value is resolved the same way in both single-file and directory mode). Building up the sequence of these records across a story's lines yields the frame chain later emitted as a DDL textchain. Any further bytes in the line's payload, beyond this first integer, are not examined by the converter.

subsection.title: Text-content lines
subsection.p: A text-content line's payload always begins with 16 bytes that are skipped without interpretation; their purpose (possibly cached per-line ruler or style state) is not established. Interpretation of the actual content, a mixture of literal text bytes and inline control codes, begins at payload byte 16 and continues to the end of the line.

Bytes with a value of 32 or more are literal text, copied directly to the output (with '"' and '\' backslash-escaped when the converter emits them inside a quoted DDL string). Bytes below 32 introduce inline control codes:

value-table.value: Single byte, no payload. Purpose undetermined.

Page/chapter/paragraph number marker. Payload: one 4-byte-aligned integer, whose low byte selects the number kind (1 = current page number, 2 = current chapter number, 4 = a numbered-list/heading value, whose specific numbering record is identified by the remaining 24 bits, a tag looked up in the numbering table; see "Paragraph and Heading Numbering").

Single byte, no payload. Paragraph break. Precisely: sets a "pending paragraph break" flag rather than acting immediately, so trailing or consecutive CTRL_M bytes do not each produce a separate empty paragraph. That flag is only checked (and, if set, turned into an actual paragraph split and cleared) at two specific points: the start of the next line record, and at a CTRL_G/CTRL_H style-stack change. It is not checked before ordinary literal text, or before CTRL_K, CTRL_R, CTRL_S, CTRL_U, or CTRL_] -- those can all occur between a CTRL_M and the point the break is actually applied, without triggering it early. See CTRL_N for the one case that discards a pending break instead of applying it.

Single byte, no payload. Forces text to continue at the top of the next frame or page. If a paragraph break is pending (see CTRL_M) when this is encountered, it is silently discarded rather than applied first: text immediately followed by CTRL_M then CTRL_N behaves as though the CTRL_M were never there.

Tab-stop marker. Payload: a 4-byte-aligned run of integers terminated by a zero value; only a single tab is emitted in the output regardless of how many integers the payload contains, so the meaning of individual entries beyond the first is undetermined.

Embedded-frame or merge-field marker. Payload: a 4-byte-aligned length integer (the total byte length of the following tagged data, including this length integer's own four bytes), followed by a tagged record whose first field is a discriminator: 1 (SEMBED) selects an embedstr record, 2 (SMERGE) selects a mergestr record; see "Embedded and merge markers" below.
Payload: two 4-byte-aligned integers, read and skipped. Purpose undetermined.

"Vertical and horizontal kerning" marker, per the source's own comment. Payload: four 4-byte-aligned integers (apparently two coordinate-like pairs), read and skipped entirely; kerning adjustments are not reproduced in the converter's output.

"Styles on" / "styles off" markers. Payload: a 4-byte-aligned count integer (the byte length of the following list, though the converter instead scans for a terminator), followed by a zero-terminated list of 4-byte-aligned integers, each holding a style-table slot number in its low byte. In the main text-writing pass, both codes are handled identically: every style currently on an internal "active styles" stack is closed (emitting a style-removal marker for each), the stack is replaced with the newly listed styles, and a style-application marker is emitted for each of those. In an earlier scan used only to determine which styles are actually used in the document, CTRL_H instead removes the listed styles from the "used" set, distinguishing it from CTRL_G in that pass only. This suggests CTRL_G marks the start, and CTRL_H the end, of a run of text using the named style(s), even though the main writer does not need to distinguish them once it knows the full replacement set at each marker.

value.name: CTRL_A, CTRL_B, CTRL_V, CTRL_W, CTRL_X, CTRL_Z

value-table.value: Payload: a zero-terminated list of 4-byte-aligned integers, in the same shape as CTRL_G/CTRL_H's list but without a preceding count. Entirely skipped by the converter; individual meanings undetermined, though their proximity to CTRL_G/CTRL_H in the control-code space makes character-level attribute markers (as opposed to named styles) a plausible, unconfirmed guess.
Not explicitly handled; treated as a single consumed byte with no special meaning.

subsection.title: Embedded and merge markers
subsection.p: Both record kinds referenced from a CTRL_S marker (see above) begin with the same discriminator field, so that only its value need be checked before choosing which structure follows:

offset-table.offset: Discriminator: 1 for an embedstr (embedded frame reference), 2 for a mergestr (merge-field reference).

subsection.p: The embedstr record (20 bytes total):

offset-table.offset: 1, identifying this as an embedstr.
Unknown.
Matches the embedtag field of the frame (see "Frame object common layout") that should be placed inline at this point in the text.
Unknown.
Unknown.

subsection.p: The mergestr record (12 bytes plus a variable-length string):

offset-table.offset: 2, identifying this as a mergestr.
Unknown.
Unknown.
Null-terminated name of the merge field, for example a database column name. Emitted in the converter's DDL output as a merge-field reference formula built from this name.

subsection.title: Repeating and chained frames
subsection.p: Ordinary (non-repeating) stories are linked to their frames purely through the frame-reference lines described above. Repeating frames (the "repeating" flag bit in the frame flags word; see "Frame flags word") are handled differently: each new frame instance that flows from a repeating master-page frame is recorded, in the order encountered, into a chain associated with that frame's dictionary entry, and a chapter's set of such chains is flushed to the output as one DDL textchain per dictionary entry once every frame on that chapter's pages has been processed. Successive uses of the same repeating frame are distinguished in the output using the "generation" counter mentioned in "Frame identifiers and epochs".

section.title: Keyboard Shortcut Encoding
section.p: A style's key field (see "Style record fixed header (stylestr)") is a RISC OS internal key code identifying the keyboard shortcut assigned to apply that style. The converter maps a subset of code values, and ranges of values, to shortcut names as follows; any value not listed produces no recognised shortcut name.

p.fixme: This section consolidates every field and code path in this chapter whose purpose is unconfirmed or entirely unknown, gathered here for convenience alongside the fuller, in-context notes given at each field's own definition.

item.p: File header: v1 (offset 0); the 188-byte block at offset 12; xx1 (offset 200); the 72-byte block at offset 204; x8, x9, x10 (offsets 316, 324); and the reason for the apparent duplication of colour2, colour3, x3, x4, x5, dict2, mdict2, and masterpages2 (see the note following the file header table, and each field's own description).

Frame object common layout: the leading word (xxxx0); most of the flags-word bits described as reserved in "Frame flags word" and "Frame group flags word"; xxxx30, xxxx32, xxxx33; and the trailing 28-byte reserved block.

Picture frame: the exact byte order of the lpi/psscreen/psx0 word; the trailing 32-byte reserved block; opcode 6 (curve) of the irregular-boundary path, and any extension sub-record kind other than the irregular boundary itself.
Section object: the leading word (xxxx0); copyprev; the 64-byte reserved block at offset 16; the 32-byte reserved block at offset 84.
Colour table: colour flags bits 2-6; the exact bit packing of the HSV channel encoding (reproduced from the conversion source but not independently confirmed); xx3, xx4, xx5.

Character and paragraph styles: roughly thirty individual "xxxNNN" bits across both presence-flags words (each listed individually at its own definition above); xxx4, xxx5; b1, b2; contents and index (plausible but unconfirmed meanings); and the "further four bytes" the source notes can apparently follow the trailing colour words.
Object dictionary: type1, type2, type3; xxx2-xxx5; len (its value is never read); xxx7; xxx9-xxx13.
EPS embedded object data: bytes 0-11 and 52-67 of the raw on-disk header (the latter is additionally overwritten in place by the converter before it can be further examined).

Text-content lines: the 16-byte preamble at the start of every line's payload; CTRL_E; the individual entries of a CTRL_R tab-stop list beyond the first; CTRL_U; CTRL_] (beyond its general description as a kerning marker); and CTRL_A, CTRL_B, CTRL_V, CTRL_W, CTRL_X, CTRL_Z in full.

Paragraph and heading numbering: styles other than decimal (types 1-5) are recognised on disk but the converter does not implement their formatted output; this is a known gap in the converter, not an unidentified part of the format.
